title: Potential Applications of Computerised Algorithms and Implementation of AI Models into Microbiological, Evolutionary and Pharmaceutical Research
content: Artificial intelligence has sharply and broadly evolved since the invention of the computer and its eventual widespread distribution throughout the world. It has led to the replacement of traditional, long-term clinical practices to computerised procedures bringing rapid results. Ultimately, this led to the development of bioinformatics, helping geneticists sequence whole genomes and proteomes within a short time frame. Subsequently, biostatisticians receive novel tools to rapidly build statistical projections in a record amount of time as well. The overall key word behind computerised advancement of biological, genetic and medical research is “time”, as bioinformatics and biotechnology represent two key “enzymes” for the “chemical reaction” of clinical research. As a result, the field of epidemiology has received a novel, all-time opportunity to rapidly build statistical projections regarding the probability of future epidemic or even pandemic outbreaks, and the scope of the current paper is to academically raise awareness of such an opportunity, and to briefly describe examples through which such process could be performed from a general, biomedical science-based perspective. The central scope of the such research efforts could be the investigation of past single-nucleotide polymorphism events that have occurred in certain polymorphic viral agents responsible for the onset of clinically powerful infectious diseases, both indirectly, through the suppression of first-line and second-line host immunity, as well as directly, through the causation of clinical disease and even decrease in the quality of the induced third-line immune activity, to bring an overall system of scientific projection that will bring above-threshold levels of accuracy in the calculation of statistical probabilities regarding the onset of future epidemics and pandemics. It is important to observe the manner microbial agents substantially contribute to the onset of significant and severe clinical infectious diseases, not only by directly inducing the disease and targeting the central, adaptive elements of the host immune system, but also by causing a transient delay in the activation of the peripheral, innate elements of the host immunity, which play a critical role in the creation of an optimal bridge of signalling to the adaptive immunity, meaning that an optimal innate immune activation process plays a crucial role in a timely and qualitative activation of the adaptive immune system.
